journeys.title: Understanding Your Anxiety
journeys.description: A 30-day guided journey to understand, manage, and reduce anxiety in everyday life.

days.title: What is anxiety, really?
days.task: Read this plain-language explainer on what anxiety is and why your body creates it.
days.source_title: What is anxiety? — Mind UK
days.reflection: After reading, write down one situation this week where you felt anxious. Just name it — no analysis needed.

days.title: How anxiety affects your body
days.task: Watch this short video on the physical symptoms of anxiety and the fight-or-flight response.
days.source_title: How anxiety affects the body — TED-Ed

days.title: Name your anxiety triggers
days.task: Write down 5 things that consistently make you feel anxious. Be specific — not 'work' but 'Monday morning emails'.
days.reflection: Keep this list. You'll come back to it on day 10.

days.title: The anxiety-breathing connection
days.task: Read about how your breathing patterns directly affect your anxiety levels.
days.source_title: How breathing affects anxiety — Calm Blog

days.title: Try box breathing
days.task: Use the Meditate tab to do a 5-minute box breathing session. Inhale 4 counts, hold 4, exhale 4, hold 4.
days.reflection: Notice how you feel before and after. Even a small shift counts.

days.title: Anxiety vs. worry — what's the difference?
days.task: Read this article on the difference between normal worry and anxiety disorder.
days.source_title: Worry vs. Anxiety — Verywell Mind

days.title: Week 1 check-in
days.task: Write 3 sentences: what you've learned this week, one thing that surprised you, and one thing you want to try next week.

days.title: What anxiety actually sounds like
days.task: Watch this honest account of living with anxiety — real voices, not clinical language.
days.source_title: Living with anxiety — BBC Ideas

days.title: The role of sleep in anxiety
days.task: Read about how poor sleep amplifies anxiety — and what to do about it.
days.source_title: Anxiety and sleep — Sleep Foundation
days.reflection: One small change: no screens 20 minutes before bed tonight. Just try it once.

days.title: Revisit your trigger list
days.task: Pull out the list you wrote on Day 3. Which triggers are within your control? Circle those. For the others — can you reduce your exposure or prepare better?

days.title: Anxious thoughts vs. facts
days.task: Read about cognitive distortions — the thinking patterns that make anxiety worse.
days.source_title: Common cognitive distortions — Psych Central

days.title: The 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique
days.task: When you next feel anxious, stop and name: 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell, 1 you can taste. Try it now as practice.

days.title: What cognitive behavioural therapy teaches us about anxiety
days.task: Watch this accessible overview of CBT techniques used to treat anxiety.
days.source_title: CBT for anxiety explained — Therapy in a Nutshell

days.title: Exercise as anxiety medicine
days.task: Read the evidence behind why physical movement is one of the most effective anxiety reducers.
days.source_title: Exercise for anxiety — Harvard Health
days.reflection: Commit to a 15-minute walk today. No phone, no podcasts — just walk.

days.title: Halfway point
days.task: You're 15 days in. Write down: one old habit that's shifting, one new thing you've tried, one thing you're still struggling with. Honest answers only.

days.title: How anxiety affects relationships
days.task: Read about how anxiety can show up in how we relate to others — and what to do about it.
days.source_title: Anxiety in relationships — Verywell Mind

days.title: The anxiety spiral — and how to break it
days.task: Watch this short explainer on how anxious thoughts spiral and the exact moment to interrupt them.
days.source_title: Breaking the anxiety spiral — Therapy in a Nutshell

days.title: Write a worry list — then close it
days.task: Set a 10-minute timer. Write every worry currently in your head. When the timer ends, fold or close the list. Tell yourself: 'I've given my worries their time. Now I'm done for today.'

days.title: Caffeine, alcohol, and anxiety
days.task: Read how common substances fuel anxiety — and what to be mindful of.
days.source_title: Caffeine and anxiety — Healthline
days.reflection: Try reducing your coffee by one cup today. Note any difference in your baseline tension.

days.title: Accepting uncertainty as an anxiety tool
days.task: Watch this talk on why accepting uncertainty (not fighting it) is a core anxiety skill.
days.source_title: How to cope with uncertainty — TED Talk (Maggie Jackson)

days.title: What has anxiety protected you from?
days.task: Anxiety often developed for a reason — it kept you alert, safe, prepared. Write down one way your anxiety has actually served you in the past. Then write whether that protection is still needed today.

days.title: Mindfulness for anxious people
days.task: Read this practical guide to mindfulness — written for people who find it hard to sit still.
days.source_title: Mindfulness for anxiety — NHS

days.title: Two-minute body scan
days.task: Sit quietly. Starting from your feet, slowly move your attention up through your body. Notice where you're holding tension. Don't try to fix it — just notice. Take two minutes.

days.title: When to get professional help
days.task: Read about the signs that anxiety may need professional support — no shame in this read.
days.source_title: When to seek help for anxiety — Mind UK
days.reflection: If any of this resonates, the AskNelson tab connects you with a counsellor today.

days.title: Self-compassion and anxiety
days.task: Watch this short video on how treating yourself with kindness — not criticism — is a clinical anxiety tool.
days.source_title: Self-compassion for anxiety — Dr. Kristin Neff

days.title: Write a letter to your anxious self
days.task: Write a short letter — 5 to 10 sentences — to the version of you that feels most anxious. Be kind. Tell them what you know now that you didn't before.

days.title: Building your personal anxiety toolkit
days.task: Read this guide to building a set of go-to strategies that work specifically for you.
days.source_title: Anxiety coping strategies — Beyond Blue

days.title: Design your toolkit
days.task: Write down your 5 personal go-to anxiety strategies from this journey. Keep it somewhere you'll find it — phone notes, back of a notebook, wherever works.

days.title: Stories of recovery
days.task: Watch real people talk about managing anxiety long-term — not curing it, but living well alongside it.
days.source_title: Living well with anxiety — Heads Together

days.title: Day 30 — your letter to yourself
days.task: Write a final reflection. How do you feel compared to Day 1? What has changed? What do you want to keep working on? Seal this somewhere and read it in 3 months.
days.reflection: You showed up for 30 days. That matters.

journeys.title: Finding Connection
journeys.description: A 30-day journey to understand loneliness, rebuild connection, and feel less alone — starting from where you are right now.

days.title: Loneliness is not the same as being alone
days.task: Read this short piece on the difference between solitude and loneliness — and why the distinction matters.
days.source_title: Loneliness vs. solitude — Psychology Today
days.reflection: Which one describes how you feel most often right now?

days.title: The loneliness epidemic
days.task: Watch this TED Talk on why loneliness has become one of the defining health issues of our time.
days.source_title: What makes a good life — Robert Waldinger TED Talk

days.title: Map your connections
days.task: Draw three circles on a page. In the inner circle, write names of people you feel truly close to. Middle circle: people you enjoy but aren't intimate with. Outer circle: acquaintances. Look at what you've drawn — what do you notice?

days.title: What loneliness does to the body
days.task: Read the science of how chronic loneliness affects physical health — not to scare you, but to show it's real.
days.source_title: The health effects of loneliness — Harvard Health

days.title: Send one message
days.task: Reach out to one person you haven't spoken to in a while. It doesn't need to be long. 'Hey, been thinking about you. Hope you're well.' That's enough.

days.title: Why connection feels hard
days.task: Read about the barriers that stop people from reaching out — fear of rejection, pride, shame — and how common they are.
days.source_title: Why is it so hard to make friends as an adult — The Atlantic

days.title: Week 1 check-in
days.task: What type of connection do you miss most — deep conversation, company, physical presence, being known? Write it down honestly.

days.title: The art of vulnerability
days.task: Watch Brené Brown's famous talk on why vulnerability is not weakness — it's the foundation of real connection.
days.source_title: The power of vulnerability — Brené Brown TED Talk

days.title: How to have a real conversation
days.task: Read this practical guide to deeper conversations — the kind that actually create connection.
days.source_title: How to have deeper conversations — Greater Good Magazine

days.title: One honest conversation
days.task: In your next conversation with someone — anyone — try to go one level deeper than you normally would. Ask something real. Share something real.
days.reflection: You don't need to overshare. One honest moment is enough.

days.title: The role of community in wellbeing
days.task: Read about how belonging to a community — any community — acts as a buffer against loneliness.
days.source_title: The importance of belonging — APA

days.title: Where could you belong?
days.task: List 3 communities, groups, or activities where you could show up regularly — a class, a club, a volunteer group, a running group. They don't need to be close yet — just where you could start.

days.title: Loneliness at work
days.task: Watch this short piece on why professional connection matters more than we admit.
days.source_title: Loneliness at work — TED Talk

days.title: Small acts, big connection
days.task: Read about micro-moments of connection — how brief positive interactions with strangers and colleagues accumulate into genuine wellbeing.
days.source_title: Micro-moments of love — Greater Good Magazine
days.reflection: Today, make eye contact and genuinely smile at three people. That's the whole task.

days.title: Halfway check-in
days.task: Has anything shifted in how you see your own loneliness? Write three sentences: where you started, where you are, where you want to go.

days.title: Loneliness and social media
days.task: Read the nuanced take on how social media can both deepen loneliness and — when used intentionally — help.
days.source_title: Social media and loneliness — Verywell Mind

days.title: Digital audit
days.task: For one day, notice every time you open social media out of boredom or loneliness. Don't try to stop — just notice. Count the moments.

days.title: On friendship in adulthood
days.task: Watch this honest conversation about why adult friendships are hard to maintain and how to invest in them properly.
days.source_title: The science of friendship — Big Think

days.title: Being a good friend
days.task: Read about what the research says makes someone a good friend — it's simpler than we think.
days.source_title: What makes a good friend — Greater Good Magazine
days.reflection: Who in your life could use you showing up as a better friend right now?

days.title: Plan something concrete
days.task: Reach out to someone and make a specific plan — coffee, a walk, a call at a specific time. Not 'we should catch up' — an actual date.

days.title: What connection means to you
days.task: Write your own definition of connection. Not what it means in general — what it personally means to feel connected. What does that feel like in your body? When did you last feel it?

days.title: Helping others as a path out of loneliness
days.task: Read about why acts of service — volunteering, helping a neighbour — are one of the most evidence-backed ways to reduce loneliness.
days.source_title: Giving and wellbeing — Action for Happiness

days.title: Loneliness is not your fault
days.task: Watch this compassionate talk that reframes loneliness not as a personal failure but as a signal — like hunger.
days.source_title: The lethality of loneliness — TED Talk (John Cacioppo)

days.title: When loneliness needs professional support
days.task: Read about when loneliness tips into something that needs more than self-help.
days.source_title: Loneliness and depression — Mind UK
days.reflection: The AskNelson tab has a counsellor booking if any of this resonates.

days.title: Do one thing in public
days.task: Go somewhere — a café, a library, a park, a gym class — not to meet anyone, just to be around people. Bring nothing to hide behind. Sit and exist alongside others for 30 minutes.

days.title: Write to a future friend
days.task: Write a short letter introducing yourself to a friend you haven't met yet. Describe what kind of friend you are, what you're looking for, and what you'd bring to the friendship.
days.reflection: This is as much about knowing yourself as about finding others.

days.title: The science of belonging
days.task: Read the research on what makes humans feel they belong — and the small, surprising things that create it.
days.source_title: The science of belonging — Greater Good Magazine

days.title: Connection in unexpected places
days.task: Watch this film on how people find community in unlikely ways — a reminder that connection doesn't have to look conventional.
days.source_title: The art of community — TED Playlist

days.title: Invest in one relationship
days.task: Choose one relationship from your connection map on Day 3 that you want to nurture. Make a concrete commitment to investing in it over the next month. Write it down.

days.title: Day 30 — you are not alone
days.task: Write your final reflection. What has changed? What do you understand about your loneliness now that you didn't before? What is one relationship you're going to invest in next month?
days.reflection: Showing up for 30 days takes courage. You did it.

journeys.title: Recovering from Burnout
journeys.description: A 30-day journey to understand burnout, recover your energy, and rebuild a sustainable relationship with work and life.

days.title: What burnout actually is
days.task: Read the WHO's definition of burnout and how it differs from stress or tiredness.
days.source_title: What is burnout? — WHO / Verywell Mind
days.reflection: Score yourself 1–10 on these three dimensions: exhaustion, cynicism, feeling ineffective. Write the numbers down.

days.title: The burnout cycle
days.task: Watch this clear explanation of how burnout builds gradually — and why it's so hard to see coming.
days.source_title: Burnout explained — Kurzgesagt

days.title: When did it start?
days.task: Try to trace your burnout backwards. When did you last feel genuinely energised by your work? What changed? Write it out — this is not about blame, it's about understanding.

days.title: The six causes of burnout
days.task: Read the research-backed framework of the six workplace factors that cause burnout. Not all of them are your fault.
days.source_title: Six causes of burnout — Christina Maslach / Mind Tools
days.reflection: Circle the 1–2 causes that apply most to you.

days.title: Do absolutely nothing for 20 minutes
days.task: No phone. No TV. No podcast. Sit or lie down and do nothing for 20 minutes. If thoughts come, let them. This is rest, not meditation.
days.reflection: Notice how uncomfortable this feels. That discomfort is data.

days.title: Why rest doesn't fix burnout
days.task: Read about why a holiday or weekend off doesn't cure burnout — and what actually does.
days.source_title: Why rest doesn't cure burnout — Harvard Business Review

days.title: Week 1 check-in
days.task: Score yourself again: exhaustion, cynicism, feeling ineffective — 1 to 10. Compare to Day 1. Write one sentence about what you've noticed.

days.title: High performance and burnout
days.task: Watch this talk on the relationship between ambition, overwork, and burnout — particularly useful if you're a high achiever.
days.source_title: Preventing burnout — TED Talk (Rahaf Harfoush)

days.title: Your nervous system and burnout
days.task: Read about how chronic stress physically changes your nervous system — and the first steps to regulate it.
days.source_title: Nervous system and burnout — Healthline

days.title: A morning without urgency
days.task: Tomorrow morning, don't look at your phone for the first 30 minutes after waking. Do something slow — make tea, stretch, sit outside. Give yourself a morning that belongs to you.

days.title: Setting limits at work
days.task: Read this practical guide to setting limits — not walls — with work demands.
days.source_title: How to set boundaries at work — Mind
days.reflection: What is one boundary you need to set this week? Be specific.

days.title: The antidote to exhaustion is not rest
days.task: Watch this short but profound talk on how wholeheartedness — not efficiency — is the cure for burnout.
days.source_title: The antidote to exhaustion — David Whyte

days.title: What do you actually value?
days.task: List your top 5 personal values — what matters most to you in life. Then list how much time you actually spent on each one last week. The gap between the two lists is worth examining.

days.title: Burnout and identity
days.task: Read about how burnout often hits people whose identity is tightly wrapped up in their work.
days.source_title: Burnout and identity — Harvard Business Review

days.title: Halfway point
days.task: Who are you outside of your job title? List 10 things about yourself that have nothing to do with work. Take as long as you need.

days.title: Sleep and burnout recovery
days.task: Read about the specific sleep changes that accelerate burnout recovery.
days.source_title: Sleep and burnout — Sleep Foundation
days.reflection: Choose one sleep habit to implement tonight: consistent bedtime, no screens 30 minutes before bed, or a wind-down routine. Pick one.

days.title: The three-item day
days.task: Today, choose only three things that matter most to get done. Not a full to-do list — three. When they're done, you're done. Let the rest wait.

days.title: Why we need to talk about burnout
days.task: Watch this candid talk from someone who experienced severe burnout — the warning signs they missed and what recovery looked like.
days.source_title: My experience with burnout — TED Talk

days.title: How to ask for help at work
days.task: Read this guide to raising workload concerns with a manager — practically and professionally.
days.source_title: How to talk to your boss about burnout — Harvard Business Review

days.title: What needs to change?
days.task: Be honest. List the structural things in your work or life that are driving your burnout. Then mark each one: Can I change this? Can I change how I relate to it? Or do I need help changing it?

days.title: The joy audit
days.task: Read about how reconnecting with enjoyment — not productivity — is a clinical burnout recovery tool.
days.source_title: Reclaiming joy — Greater Good Magazine
days.reflection: Write down three activities that used to bring you joy. When did you last do any of them?

days.title: Do something just for joy
days.task: Today, do one thing from your joy list — even a small version. Not because it's productive. Not because it makes you better at your job. Just because it's enjoyable.

days.title: Redefining success
days.task: Watch this talk on the cultural drivers of overwork — and what a different relationship with success could look like.
days.source_title: Redefining success — Arianna Huffington TED Talk

days.title: When to get professional support
days.task: Read about the signs that burnout has crossed into something that needs a professional — a counsellor, coach, or doctor.
days.source_title: When burnout needs professional help — Mind UK
days.reflection: If any of this matches your experience, the AskNelson tab can connect you with a counsellor or coach today.

days.title: Protect one hour
days.task: Block one hour in your calendar this week that is completely yours. Not a meeting. Not a task. Not 'catch up'. Your hour. Guard it.

days.title: Your sustainable pace
days.task: Describe — in writing — what a sustainable week looks like for you. Not ideal, but sustainable. What time do you start? What time do you stop? What do you protect? What do you let go of?

days.title: Recovery is not linear
days.task: Read about why burnout recovery takes longer than people expect — and how to be compassionate with yourself on hard days.
days.source_title: Burnout recovery timeline — Psychology Today

days.title: Write your recovery commitments
days.task: Write three specific commitments to yourself for the next 90 days — things you will do differently to prevent burnout returning. Make them concrete, not vague.

days.title: Building a life that doesn't burn you out
days.task: Watch this talk on intentional living — designing your work and life from the inside out rather than reacting to demands.
days.source_title: Designing your life — Bill Burnett TED Talk

days.title: Day 30 — you came back to yourself
days.task: Final reflection. How does your energy compare to Day 1? What do you know about yourself now? Read the commitments you wrote on Day 28. Sign them.
days.reflection: Recovery takes time. But you started. That's not nothing.

journeys.title: Moving Through Grief
journeys.description: A 30-day companion for people navigating loss — of a person, a relationship, a job, or anything that mattered.

days.title: Grief is not a problem to solve
days.task: Read this compassionate piece that reframes grief not as something to fix but as something to move through.
days.source_title: What grief really is — David Kessler
days.reflection: There's no right way to grieve. You're doing it the right way for you.

days.title: The stages of grief — a more honest look
days.task: Watch this short piece that updates the famous 'five stages' model with what we actually know now about how grief works.
days.source_title: Rethinking grief — TED Talk (Nora McInerny)

days.title: Name your loss
days.task: Write about what you've lost — not just the person or thing, but what their absence means. What did they give you? What has changed in your daily life? What future have you lost alongside them?
days.reflection: Take as long as you need. There's no word count here.

days.title: How grief lives in the body
days.task: Read about the physical experience of grief — why you feel it in your chest, your stomach, your sleep.
days.source_title: The body in grief — Verywell Mind

days.title: Be gentle with your body today
days.task: Do something kind for your body today. It could be sleep, a slow walk, a warm bath, eating something nourishing. Grief is physical work. Your body is working hard.

days.title: Grief and isolation
days.task: Read about why people pull away from others when grieving — and the cost of doing so alone.
days.source_title: Grief and loneliness — Psychology Today

days.title: Week 1 check-in
days.task: In one sentence: how are you, honestly? Not 'fine'. The real answer.

days.title: What people wish they knew about grief
days.task: Watch this honest conversation between people who have experienced significant loss.
days.source_title: The gift of grief — TED Talk

days.title: Continuing bonds — staying connected to who you've lost
days.task: Read about the theory of continuing bonds — that healthy grief doesn't mean moving on, it means finding a new relationship with what you've lost.
days.source_title: Continuing bonds theory — What's Your Grief

days.title: A letter you won't send
days.task: Write a letter to whoever or whatever you've lost. Say what you didn't get to say, or what you need to say now. You will not send this. It's for you.

days.title: Complicated grief
days.task: Read about when grief becomes 'complicated' — when it intensifies or gets stuck rather than shifting over time.
days.source_title: Complicated grief — Mayo Clinic
days.reflection: If any of this applies to you, please use the AskNelson tab to speak to someone.

days.title: Grief and gratitude — can they coexist?
days.task: Watch this nuanced talk on whether it's possible — or even useful — to hold gratitude alongside grief.
days.source_title: Good grief — TED Talk (Lesley Lacny)

days.title: What you are grateful for
days.task: Write 5 things about the person, relationship, or situation you lost that you are grateful for. Not things you miss — things you're grateful to have had.

days.title: How to support yourself when you're grieving
days.task: Read this practical guide to self-care during grief — especially when getting through the day is already hard enough.
days.source_title: Self-care in grief — What's Your Grief

days.title: Halfway — what has shifted?
days.task: Not 'are you better?' but 'what has shifted?'. Write one thing that feels different than it did on Day 1.

days.title: Grief anniversaries and triggers
days.task: Read about grief triggers — dates, smells, songs, places — and how to prepare for and navigate them.
days.source_title: Grief triggers — What's Your Grief

days.title: Create a small ritual
days.task: Create a small ritual to honour what you've lost. Light a candle on a certain day. Visit a place that mattered. Cook their favourite meal. Small rituals give grief somewhere to go.

days.title: Grief and work — navigating both
days.task: Watch this candid account of what it's like to grieve while also needing to function at work.
days.source_title: Grieving and working — TED Talk

days.title: How other cultures grieve
days.task: Read about how different cultures and traditions approach grief — some have a lot to teach us.
days.source_title: How different cultures grieve — HuffPost

days.title: What has this loss taught you?
days.task: Not 'what is the silver lining'. But honestly — what has this experience revealed about yourself, your values, or what matters to you? Even difficult answers are valid here.

days.title: Post-traumatic growth
days.task: Read about post-traumatic growth — the genuine, evidence-based phenomenon of people finding meaning after profound loss.
days.source_title: Post-traumatic growth — Greater Good Magazine
days.reflection: This is not 'everything happens for a reason'. It's about what we build from what happens.

days.title: Share a memory
days.task: Share a memory of what you've lost with someone who will listen. A friend, a family member, a colleague. Just one memory. Grief carried alone is heavier.

days.title: We don't 'move on' — we move forward
days.task: Watch this powerful short talk reframing what it means to live after loss.
days.source_title: Moving forward with grief — TED Talk (Nora McInerny)

days.title: When grief needs professional support
days.task: Read about the signs that grief would benefit from professional support — and why asking for help is not weakness.
days.source_title: Getting help for grief — NHS
days.reflection: The AskNelson tab has a counsellor available if you need to talk.

days.title: Give yourself permission
days.task: Write yourself a short note giving yourself explicit permission — to grieve, to feel better, to laugh, to be sad again, to take as long as you need. Sign it.

days.title: What do you want to carry forward?
days.task: Write about what you want to carry forward from this loss — a value, a lesson, a way of being, something they stood for. How will they remain part of who you are?

days.title: Life after loss
days.task: Read about how people rebuild — not to the same life, but a different one that makes room for what happened.
days.source_title: Rebuilding after loss — What's Your Grief

days.title: Finding meaning
days.task: Watch this talk on how humans find meaning — and how meaning can exist even inside profound pain.
days.source_title: The search for meaning — Emily Esfahani Smith TED Talk

days.title: Do something that honours them
days.task: Do something today that honours what or who you've lost. Plant something. Cook something. Write something. Give something. Make it intentional.

days.title: Day 30 — still here
days.task: Write a final reflection. You came to this journey carrying something heavy. Write about what you've learned, what has softened, and how you want to move forward. Then write these words at the end: I am still here.
days.reflection: You showed up every day. That takes real strength.
